sections.title: 3. The O(n log n) Patience Method
4. Where LIS Hides in Other Problems
5. How to Recognise and Approach LIS

blocks.text: The Longest Increasing Subsequence, or LIS, is a classic DP problem that shows up constantly, both directly and hidden inside other problems.
The task: given an array, find the length of the longest subsequence whose values are strictly increasing. A subsequence keeps the original order but is allowed to skip elements.

blocks.caption: From the array we pick the longest run of increasing values, keeping order

blocks.text: A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more elements without reordering the ones that remain. This is different from a subarray, which must be contiguous.
For the array 10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, one longest increasing subsequence is 2, 3, 7 with length 3. Notice we skipped elements, but we never changed their order.

items: LIS asks for the longest strictly increasing subsequence

blocks.text: Define dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at index i. Every subsequence must end somewhere, so the answer is the largest value in the dp array.
To compute dp[i], look at every earlier index j. If a[j] is smaller than a[i], then a[i] can extend the subsequence that ended at j.
This is O(n squared) time, which is fine for a few thousand elements but too slow when n is large.

content.title: 3. The O(n log n) Patience Method

blocks.text: There is a beautiful faster approach. We keep an array called tails, where tails[k] holds the smallest possible value that can end an increasing subsequence of length k plus one.

blocks.caption: For each value, append it if it beats every tail, otherwise replace the first tail that is not smaller
blocks.alt: The On log n Patience Method

blocks.text: For each incoming value, if it is larger than everything in tails we append it and the LIS grows. Otherwise we binary search for the first tail that is not smaller and overwrite it, keeping tails as small as possible.

Careful:

The tails array gives the correct length of the LIS, but it is not itself a valid LIS. If you need the actual sequence, track predecessor indices separately.

content.title: 4. Where LIS Hides in Other Problems

blocks.text: Many problems are LIS wearing a disguise. Spotting the reduction is the win.

items: Russian Doll Envelopes: sort by width, then run LIS on heights.
Longest Increasing Path patterns: ordering constraints that reduce to increasing chains.
Number of LIS: count how many longest subsequences exist, an extension of the O(n squared) DP.
Longest Bitonic Subsequence: LIS from the left combined with LIS from the right.

blocks.text: When a problem asks for the longest chain under some ordering, think LIS first.

content.title: 5. How to Recognise and Approach LIS

blocks.text: Use this quick checklist when a problem smells like LIS.

items: Are you asked for the longest chain where each element beats the previous under some rule?
Can you keep order and skip elements freely? That means subsequence, not subarray.
Start with the O(n squared) dp[i] ends here formulation to get correctness.
If n is large, switch to the O(n log n) tails method with binary search.
If you need the actual sequence, store predecessors while you build.

blocks.text: Master both forms. The quadratic one is easy to reason about, and the logarithmic one is what you reach for when the input is big.
